The first time I saw the ocean, I was six years old. My family had driven for hours—past dusty fields and sleepy towns—until the highway crested a hill and there it was: an endless blue expanse stretching to the horizon, waves crashing like slow thunder. I remember standing on the shore, toes sinking into wet sand, the salt tang in the air making my nose wrinkle. The ocean didn’t care about my smallness. It didn’t care about anything, really. It just *was*—powerful, indifferent, beautiful.

That moment taught me something quiet but profound: the world is vast, and I am small. But smallness isn’t weakness. It’s a reminder to pay attention. To listen to the rhythm of the waves, to notice the way light fractures on water, to feel the weight of the wind. It’s a lesson in humility, but also in wonder.

Years later, I still return to the ocean when I need to remember. When life feels like a crowded room, the sea is a place of solitude. When I’m overwhelmed by noise, the waves offer a steady, rhythmic silence. And when I’m afraid of not being enough, the ocean whispers: *You are part of something larger. You belong here.*

I don’t know if the ocean knows I’m there when I visit. But I know I’m changed by the encounter. Every time. The world doesn’t need to acknowledge us to matter. It just needs us to notice it back.
